facts.claim: Gingival health on an intact periodontium: no attachment loss, probing depths of 3 mm or less (no pseudo pockets), bleeding on probing (BOP) at fewer than 10% of sites, no radiographic bone loss.

facts.claim: Plaque-induced gingivitis (intact periodontium or reduced periodontium in a non-periodontitis patient): BOP at 10% of sites or more with probing depths of 3 mm or less and no periodontitis.
facts.conditions: Gingivitis = BOP at 10% or more with probing depths ≤3 mm (Chapple p. S73, Table 1); the threshold quote is the health definition's mirror image.

gingivitis is defined as > 30% bleeding sites

facts.claim: Successfully treated, stable periodontitis patient: health = all probing depths 4 mm or less with no site of 4 mm or more that bleeds, BOP under 10%; gingivitis in such a patient = BOP at 10% or more at sites of 3 mm or less. A 4 mm site that bleeds is no longer a "closed pocket". The patient remains a periodontitis patient for life.

cites.quote: Where the probing depth is 4 mm or higher with bleeding, this is no longer a “closed pocket.”
the treated and stable periodontitis patient with current gingival health remains at increased risk of recurrent periodontitis

facts.claim: Three forms of periodontitis are recognized: periodontitis, necrotizing periodontitis, and periodontitis as a direct manifestation of systemic disease; the "chronic" vs "aggressive" split was dropped.

cites.quote: Three forms of periodontitis have been identified: (1) periodontitis, (2) necrotising periodontitis, (3) periodontitis as a direct manifestation of systemic diseases.
evidence to support differentiating “chronic” and “aggressive” periodontitis

facts.claim: A patient is a periodontitis case when interdental CAL is detectable at 2 or more non-adjacent teeth, or buccal/oral CAL of 3 mm or more with pocketing over 3 mm is found at 2 or more teeth, and the CAL cannot be explained by non-periodontal causes (traumatic recession, cervical caries, distal of a second molar from third-molar malposition or extraction, an endodontic lesion draining through the marginal periodontium, a vertical root fracture).

cites.quote: Interdental CAL is detectable at ≥2 non-adjacent teeth, or • Buccal/oral CAL of ≥3mm with pocketing of >3mm is detectable at ≥2 teeth

1. Gingival recession of traumatic origin; 2. Dental caries extending in the cervical area of the tooth; 3. The presence of CAL on the distal aspect of a second molar and associated with malposition or extraction of a third molar

facts.claim: Stage is set first by interdental CAL at the site of greatest loss; if CAL is unavailable, use radiographic bone loss (RBL). Tooth loss from periodontitis can modify the stage, and one or more complexity factors can shift the stage higher.

cites.quote: If CAL is not available, radiographic bone loss (RBL) should be used. Tooth loss due to periodontitis may modify stage definition. One or more complexity factors may shift the stage to a higher level.

facts.claim: Severity by stage: Stage I: CAL 1-2 mm; RBL coronal third (<15%); no tooth loss from periodontitis. Stage II: CAL 3-4 mm; RBL coronal third (15%-33%); no tooth loss. Stage III: CAL 5 mm or more; RBL to the middle third of the root and beyond; tooth loss of 4 teeth or fewer. Stage IV: CAL 5 mm or more; RBL to the middle third and beyond; tooth loss of 5 teeth or more.

cites.quote: Interdental CAL (at site of greatest loss) 1 – 2 mm 3 – 4 mm ≥5 mm ≥5 mm RBL Coronal third (<15%) Coronal third (15% - 33%) Extending to middle third of root and beyond
Tooth loss (due to periodontitis) No tooth loss ≤4 teeth ≥5 teeth

facts.claim: Complexity: Stage I: max probing depth 4 mm or less, mostly horizontal bone loss. Stage II: max probing depth 5 mm or less, mostly horizontal bone loss. Stage III (in addition to stage II complexity): probing depths 6 mm or more; vertical bone loss 3 mm or more; furcation involvement class II or III; moderate ridge defects. Stage IV (in addition to stage III complexity): need for complex rehabilitation because of masticatory dysfunction, secondary occlusal trauma (tooth mobility degree 2 or more), severe ridge defects, bite collapse/drifting/flaring, fewer than 20 remaining teeth (10 opposing pairs).

facts.claim: Grading estimates rate of progression, response to standard therapy, and possible systemic impact. Start by assuming grade B and look for evidence to move to A or C.

Clinicians should initially assume grade B disease and seek specific evidence to shift to grade A or C.

facts.claim: Direct evidence (radiographic bone loss or CAL over 5 years) is used whenever available: A = no loss over 5 years; B = less than 2 mm over 5 years; C = 2 mm or more over 5 years.

cites.quote: Primary criteria No loss over 5 years <2 mm over 5 years ≥2 mm over 5 years

facts.claim: Indirect evidence, % bone loss divided by age: A = under 0.25; B = 0.25 to 1.0; C = over 1.0. Case phenotype: A = heavy biofilm with little destruction; B = destruction in line with biofilm; C = destruction exceeds what the biofilm would predict, or patterns suggesting rapid progression or early onset.

facts.claim: "Biologic width" is renamed supracrestal tissue attachment (junctional epithelium plus supracrestal connective tissue); placing restoration margins within the supracrestal connective-tissue attachment is associated with inflammation and loss of support.

cites.quote: The term “biologic width” is replaced by “supracrestal tissue attachment”, consisting of junctional-epithelium and supracrestal connective tissue.

facts.claim: Peri-implant health: no clinical signs of inflammation, no bleeding/suppuration on gentle probing, no increase in probing depth over previous exams, no bone loss (beyond initial remodeling). No range of probing depths defines health, and health can exist around implants with reduced bone support.

cites.quote: Peri-implant health is characterised by the absence of clinical signs of inflammation, such as swelling, redness, and BoP. It is not possible, however, to define a range of probing depths that are compatible with health.
peri-implant health can exist around implants with reduced bone support

facts.claim: Peri-implant mucositis: bleeding and/or suppuration on gentle probing with no bone loss beyond initial remodeling; plaque is the cause, and it can resolve when plaque control is restored.

cites.quote: Peri-implant health Peri-implant mucositis Peri-implantitis No BoP BoP BoP No bone loss* No bone loss* Bone loss*

facts.claim: Peri-implantitis: bleeding and/or suppuration on gentle probing, increased probing depth compared with previous exams, and bone loss beyond initial remodeling.

cites.quote: Peri-implantitis sites exhibit clinical signs of inflammation including bleeding on probing and/or suppuration, increased probing depths and/or recession of the mucosal margin, and radiographic bone loss compared to previous examinations.

facts.claim: Without previous exam data, peri-implantitis can be diagnosed from bleeding/suppuration on gentle probing plus probing depths of 6 mm or more plus bone levels 3 mm or more apical to the most coronal part of the intraosseous portion of the implant.
facts.conditions: The 6 mm probing-depth part of the rule is in the same paragraph (quote not yet added).

cites.quote: bone levels ≥3mm apical of the most coronal portion of the intra-osseous part of the implant, together with bleeding and/or suppuration on probing, are consistent with the diagnosis of peri-implantitis

facts.claim: Mucositis is assumed to precede peri-implantitis; peri-implantitis progresses faster than periodontitis, in a non-linear, accelerating pattern. Strong evidence links a history of severe periodontitis, poor plaque control and missed maintenance to peri-implantitis; evidence for smoking and diabetes is inconclusive.

cites.quote: The progression of peri-implantitis is faster than that observed in periodontitis and occurs in a non-linear and accelerating pattern.

an increased risk for peri-implantitis in patients who have a history of severe periodontitis. Data identifying smoking and diabetes as potential risk indicators for peri-implantitis are inconclusive.

facts.claim: Clinicians should record baseline radiographs and probing after the implant prosthesis is completed; epidemiologic bone-loss thresholds should exceed the mean measurement error of 0.5 mm.

cites.quote: Bone loss should be reported using thresholds exceeding the measurement error (mean 0.5mm).

facts.claim: Gingival phenotype (thickness and width of keratinized gingiva) is now part of the classification; recession is described by recession depth, gingival thickness, keratinized tissue width, whether the CEJ is detectable (class A detectable / B not) and whether a cervical step over 0.5 mm is present (+/-).

cites.quote: Step = root-surface concavity (Class + = presence of a cervical step > 0.5mm. Class – = absence of a cervical step > 0.5mm)

facts.claim: Cairo recession types: RT1 = recession with no interproximal attachment loss (interproximal CEJ not visible); RT2 = interproximal attachment loss less than or equal to the buccal attachment loss; RT3 = interproximal attachment loss greater than the buccal attachment loss.

cites.quote: RT1 -- REC with no loss of interproximal CAL -- Interproximal CEJ is not visible RT2 -- REC with loss of interproximal CAL -- Interproximal loss of CAL is less than or equal to buccal C

facts.claim: Glickman (1953) furcation grades: I = incipient, suprabony pocket, slight furcal bone loss; II = loss of interradicular bone with pocketing but part of the bone/PDL remains (cul-de-sac, not through); III = through-and- through; IV = through-and-through with recession so the furcation is clearly visible.

cites.quote: Grade III: Through-and-through lesion. Grade IV: Through-and-through lesion with gingival recession, leading to a clearly visible furcation area.

facts.claim: Hamp, Nyman and Lindhe (1975), horizontal attachment loss in the furcation: degree I = under 3 mm; degree II = over 3 mm but not the total width; degree III = through-and-through.

cites.quote: Degree I: horizontal attachment loss < 3 mm of the total width of the furcation area. Degree II: horizontal attachment loss > 3 mm but not encompassing the total width of the furcation area.

facts.claim: Tarnow and Fletcher vertical subclass (from the fornix): A = 3 mm or less; B = 4-6 mm; C = 7 mm or more.

cites.quote: Subclass A: vertical bone loss 3 mm or less. Subclass B: vertical bone loss from 4 to 6 mm. Subclass C: bone loss from the fornix of 7 mm or more.

facts.claim: Miller mobility index: 0 = physiologic; 1 = first sign of more-than-normal movement; 2 = up to 1 mm buccolingually; 3 = over 1 mm buccolingually and/or depressible (vertical movement). Grades 1-2 are horizontal only; grade 3 includes vertical movement. Note: the 2017 staging chart uses "mobility degree 2 or more" as a stage IV complexity factor (PS-5).
facts.conditions: The review's prose says Miller grade 2 may include 'possible vertical or axial displacement', which disagrees with the usual teaching (grades 1-2 horizontal, grade 3 adds vertical/depressible) and its own table. Key only 'grade 3 includes vertical movement'; don't key the 1 mm cut-off or grade 2's direction until a primary source is opened.

cites.quote: Grade 3 signifies severe mobility, where the tooth exhibits significant movement, both horizontally and vertically
